### `mkSig`

```
mkSig : ExL a -> ExL (Sig a)
```

"A value, later" becomes "a signal, later" — each arrival extends the
signal by one instant.  Every signal fed by a channel starts here, and
`:::` turns the result into a signal with a value *now*.


### `Functor Sig`  <sub>instance</sub>

```
instance Functor Sig where
```

**A signal is a container of the thing it carries**, so changing what it
carries is `map` and nothing else.  `map f s` is the same node the
engine always emitted — `mapSig` is still what it is written in terms
of, and is internal below — and the name is now the one `List` and
`Maybe` already answer to.

Statically resolved, which is what makes it admissible at audio rate:
`Functor Sig` has no context, so its dictionary is a constant and
`elaborate.resolve_static_methods` turns the projection into a direct
call to `__Functor_Sig_map__` before the fragment ever sees it.  That
name is a signal former in `audiograph.FORMERS`, beside `mapSig`.


### `scan`

```
scan : (b -> a -> b) -> b -> Sig a -> Sig b
```

**State over time.**  `scan f z s` holds `z` now and `f z (head s)` at
the next instant — an accumulator folded over the signal as it arrives.
Ordinary guarded recursion: the recursive call sits under `delay`, so the
result is productive by construction.  An oscillator's phase, a filter's
memory and a game's world are all this.


### `Zip Sig`  <sub>instance</sub>

```
instance Zip Sig where
```

**Two signals meet.**  `zip f s t` is `f` of the two, instant by
instant — the node a synth reaches for whenever one signal has to see
another, and the shape `Num (Sig Float)`'s `+` is written in terms of.

Statically resolved, like `map` above and for the same reason: `Zip Sig`
has no context, so `__Zip_Sig_zip__` is a signal former in
`audiograph.FORMERS` and the fragment sees the node it always saw.


### `Both`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Both a b := Both a b
```

Two things at once — what a lift over more than two signals is built
from.

`zipSig` combines *two* signals and there is no three-signal former, so
`!f x y z` pairs its arguments up and takes the pairs apart again at the
end.  A **record** rather than a tuple, because the extractor lays out
`Int`, `Float` and declared data types and nothing else (`fixme.md`
F95) — the same reason a `voices` bank generates its own `Part` records
to fold k channels with binary zips.

A declaration and nothing else: the `zipSig` that builds one is given a
*lambda*, because a step function is emitted once at one type and a
named pairer would have to serve every element type a program lifts
over.


### `feedback`

```
feedback n f s : Int -> (Float -> Float -> Float) -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A delay line with a fold around it** — `scan` with a longer arm.

    scan       f z s :  out[t] = f (out[t-1], s[t])
    feedback n f   s :  out[t] = f (out[t-n], s[t])

The step sees what left the line `n` samples ago and this instant's
input, and what it returns is both the output *and* what goes back into
the line.  That is a feedback comb, an echo with repeats, a Schroeder
allpass, and therefore a reverb:

    echo n g s = feedback n (y x => x + g * y) s

**`n` is fixed before the program runs.**  The state is that many
samples wide and the engine has no allocator, so `feedback (seconds
0.25) …` is fine — it folds to a number — and a length that varies is
refused with that sentence.

No cycle in the graph, which is why this is the first delay primitive
rather than the general one: the loop is *inside* the node exactly as a
`scan`'s is.  `spec/delaylines.md` is the design, and `loop` below is
the same node with a *filter* in the line.

**The definition below is the oracle's, not the engine's.**  Like every
other former in this file, the audio backend recognises the name and
emits a node; the body is what `render` runs to produce the samples the
engine is checked against, and it carries the line as an ordinary list
because that is a thing the interpreter can do and the engine cannot.


### `tap`

```
tap n pos s : Int -> Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A delay line you read at a moving position** — the other half of
`spec/delaylines.md`, and the one that composes.

    tap n pos s

`s` goes in, `pos` is how many samples back to read it from, and `n` is
the furthest back it can reach.  The position is a **signal** and may be
fractional — the read is interpolated between the two samples either
side — which is what chorus, flanger and vibrato are: a delay of a few
milliseconds with an LFO on the position.

A plain delay is this at a constant: `tap n (!(toFloat n)) s`.  There is
no `delay` beside it because a delay *is* a tap that does not move.

**The position is clamped to 1 .. n-1**, and the lower bound is not
fussiness.  A tap that could hand back the sample it was given this
instant would let a cycle close with nothing in it — and reading at
least one sample back is exactly what makes this node's output a
function of its *state*, which is what a feedback path leaving the node
and coming back would have to close through.  `loop` needs none of
that: its line is inside the node, as `feedback`'s is.

The definition below is the oracle's, as `feedback`'s is: the audio
backend knows the name and emits a node, and this is what `render` runs
to produce the samples that node is checked against.


### `slide`

```
slide n f pos s : Int -> (Float -> Float -> Float) -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A delay line that bends** — `tap`'s moving, interpolated read, closed
into `feedback`'s loop.  The ring holds the node's *own* output, the
position says how far back this instant reaches into it, and the step
folds what it finds there with the input:

    feedback n f     s :  out[t] = f (out[t - n],      s[t])
    slide    n f pos s :  out[t] = f (out[t - pos[t]], s[t])

`pos` is a **signal**, in samples, and may be fractional — the read is
interpolated between the two samples either side, exactly as `tap`'s
is.  That one difference is a sliding Karplus-Strong string, a waveguide
whose pitch is a signal, an echo whose time warbles like tape: every
feedback instrument whose *length* wants to move, which `feedback`
cannot do (its slot is its cursor) and `tap` alone cannot either (its
loop would have to leave the node, and the graph refuses the cycle).

The position is clamped to 1 .. n-1, as `tap`'s is and for `tap`'s
reason: reading at least one sample back is what makes the value a
function of the *state*, so the loop always has a sample of delay in
it.  `n` is fixed before the program runs — it is the ring's width and
the furthest the position can reach, so give a sliding pitch its lowest
note's room.

The definition below is the oracle's, as its three siblings' are: the
audio backend recognises the name and emits a node, and this is what
`render` runs to produce the samples that node is checked against.


### `scope`

```
scope label s : String -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A scope on a signal** — `spec/scope.md`.  Identity on the sound:
what flows through is exactly what flowed in, and the label names
the window of recent samples the host keeps on the way past, for a
canvas to draw.  The audio backend knows the name and emits a node
whose ring is a delay line's; this body is the oracle's truth that
a scope changes nothing it touches.


### `spectro`

```
spectro label s : String -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A spectrogram on a signal** — the scope's second reader
(`spec/scope.md`): the same window, shown by frequency instead of
by time.  Identity on the sound like `scope`; the label names the
window, and the margin draws magnitude bars where a scope draws
its trace.


### `loop`

```
loop n f z s : Int -> (b -> b -> Float -> b) -> b -> Sig Float -> Sig b
```

**A delay line with a filter in it** — `feedback`, plus where the step
was an instant ago.

    scan       f z s :  st[t] = f          st[t-1]  s[t]
    feedback n f   s :  st[t] = f  st[t-n]          s[t]
    loop     n f z s :  st[t] = f  st[t-1] st[t-n]  s[t]

One ring of `n` states carries both arms: the slot about to be
overwritten is `n` instants old, the one written before it is one
instant old.  At `n` of 1 those are the same slot and this *is*
`feedback` — with a state of your choosing rather than a bare sample.

The second arm is what a plucked string needs.  Karplus-Strong averages
the two samples that left the line, and the older of the pair is not
something `feedback`'s step can reach, so the state carries it forward:

    Wire := Wire Float Float      #: the sample out, and the one before

    wireStep : Wire -> Wire -> Float -> Wire
    wireStep prev old x = case prev of
        Wire y p -> case old of
            Wire yn q -> Wire (x + 0.5 * (yn + p)) yn

    wireOut : Wire -> Float
    wireOut st = case st of
        Wire y p -> y

    pluck n s = map wireOut (loop n wireStep (Wire 0.0 0.0) s)

**The names matter here**, and not for taste: `synth.ges` declares its
own `Ks` for `string`, the library is prepended to every program, and a
second declaration of a name it already has is a duplicate rather than a
shadow.  Copying this example verbatim is why it is not called `Ks`.

`string` is this with the pitch and a decay worked out for you, and
`damped` is the same shape with a lowpass in the line.

That is a string of `n` samples' round trip — the rate over `n`
hertz — excited by whatever `s` is, and the averaging is a lowpass, so
the harmonics die before the fundamental does, as they do on a string.
Put a different filter in the step and the line becomes a waveguide.

**`n` is fixed before the program runs**, as `feedback`'s is, and the
state is `n` copies of whatever `z` is — a wide state times a long line
is a lot of memory, and it is spent whether or not the line is full.

No cycle in the graph: the loop is inside the node, as `scan`'s and
`feedback`'s are.  A feedback path that has to go *out* through other
nodes and back is what `tap` is for.

The definition below is the oracle's, as `feedback`'s and `tap`'s are:
the audio backend recognises the name and emits a node, and this is what
`render` runs to produce the samples that node is checked against.

```
gain g s : Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

## Internals

**Not callable from another file.**  Listed so that a name you meet in a stack trace or a definition can be looked up.


#### `mapSig`

```
mapSig : (a -> b) -> Sig a -> Sig b
```

Change what a signal carries, one instant at a time.


#### `zipSig`

```
zipSig : (a -> b -> c) -> Sig a -> Sig b -> Sig c
```

**The one `Zip Sig` is built out of**, and the hard part of it.

Two signals need not tick together — each has its own clock — so this
cannot simply pair up their tails.  `sync` reports which of the two
arrived, and the one that did not keeps the signal it already had:

  * `SyncLeft s2`     — only the left advanced; carry the old right.
  * `SyncRight t2`    — only the right advanced; carry the old left.
  * `SyncBoth s2 t2`  — both did.

Carrying the old one over is sound precisely because a signal is a *cell*
overwritten in place: the one that did not tick still holds what it held,
and there is nothing stale to read.


#### `lineZero`

```
lineZero n : Int -> List Float
```

`n` samples of silence — the line before anything has entered it.


#### `lineOut`

```
lineOut buf : List Float -> Float
```

What left the line `n` samples ago: the last element, or silence while
the line is still filling.


#### `lineStep`

```
lineStep f buf x : (Float -> Float -> Float) -> List Float -> Float -> List Float
```

One sample: read the oldest, fold it with the input, and put the result
in at the near end.  The list is newest-first, so "oldest" is the last
and dropping it is what makes the line a fixed length.


#### `lineOldest`

```
lineOldest buf : List Float -> Float
```


#### `lineButLast`

```
lineButLast buf : List a -> List a
```

Polymorphic because `loop`'s ring holds whole states rather than
samples; dropping the far end is the same operation either way.


#### `tapPush`

```
tapPush buf x : List Float -> Float -> List Float
```

The newest sample at the near end, and the far end falls off — so the
list is `[s[t], s[t-1], …]` and index `d` is `d` samples back.


#### `tapRead`

```
tapRead buf d : List Float -> Float -> Float
```

Read at `d` samples back, interpolating between the two either side.

Clamped to 1 .. n-1: index 0 is *this* instant's sample, which a delay
must not return, and n-1 is as far as the line reaches.

```

```

```

```

```
SlideIn := SlideIn Float Float
```

The input and the position, folded through one scan — its own record,
not `Both`, for the reason `synth.ges` gives at `OnePoleIn`: a
constructor's layout is chosen by tag, so one record at two
instantiations in a graph collides in the code generator.

```
slideHead buf : List Float -> Float
```

What the step just wrote — the node's output is this instant's sample,
as `loop`'s is, not the far end of the ring as `feedback`'s is.

```

```


#### `loopZero`

```
loopZero n z : Int -> a -> List a
```

`n` copies of the initial state — the ring before anything has run.


#### `loopPrev`

```
loopPrev z buf : a -> List a -> a
```

Where the step was an instant ago: the near end, or the initial state
while nothing has been written yet.


#### `loopOld`

```
loopOld z buf : a -> List a -> a
```

What left the line `n` instants ago: the far end, or the initial state.


#### `loopStep`

```
loopStep f z buf x : (a -> a -> Float -> a) -> a -> List a -> Float -> List a
```

One instant.  The step sees both ends and this instant's input, and what
it returns goes on the near end while the far end falls off.


#### `addSig`

```
addSig a b : Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

Add two signals — the reason `zipSig` was wanted.  Two oscillators can be
two signals now, rather than two fields of one state.


#### `mulSig`

```
mulSig a b : Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

Multiply two signals — a gain you can *turn*.

`gain` takes a `Float`, and a `Float` is a constant the extractor folds
into the graph as a literal; a knob is a `Sig Float`, so it cannot go
there and `gain level s` does not typecheck.  This is what does: a
parameter that varies is a second signal, and combining two signals is
`zipSig`.  The same shape is an amplitude envelope, a tremolo, or one
oscillator's output used as another's volume — none of which needed a
combinator of their own.


#### `subSig`

```
subSig a b : Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

Subtract one signal from another.  Here for the same reason `addSig` is,
and because `Num (Sig Float)` needs all three to be a `Num` at all.
